newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy upbeat on Euro deal, but efforts to go on.
newsitem.headline: Italy upbeat on Euro deal, but efforts to go on.

text.p: Italian newspapers on Tuesday greeted news that European Union leaders had patched up a potentially disastrous dispute over the planned single currency with delight, but urged Rome to step up its efforts to qualify.

"Way clear for the euro," headlined dailies La Repubblica and La Stampa, declaring the deal on a stability pact designed to keep budgets in trim as a good omen for the targeted 1999 launch of economic and monetary union (EMU).
Italy's bond market surged on the Amsterdam summit euphoria. The lira and stock market also firmed.
La Stampa described the agreement, which had risked overshadowing the two-day summit and scuppering the whole project, as an "honourable compromise".
France and Germany fell out over the stability pact after France said attention to the high EU jobless rate should not be ignored in order to concentrate on budgetary rigour.
EU leaders agreed to add a resolution on employment, something La Repubblica said made it "a more humane pact".
"The immediate satisfaction remains of having involved all of Europe in a debate on unemployment, the most painful of problems," the newspaper said.
Corriere della Sera newspaper advised Italy, which is desperate to become a founder member of the new currency, the euro, to take home a message from Amsterdam.
"If Italy wants to make the most of renewed French support to join the first group of monetary union, it has to adopt structural measures to defy 1998 deficit forecasts," it said.
The European Commission itself has forecast that Italy will not be able to keep its deficit-to-Gross Domestic Product ratio to the three percent EMU target next year.

But budgetary woes in Germany and greater caution over the euro in Paris since the election of Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin have fuelled hopes that Italy will be among a broader group of countries to launch the euro on softer terms.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi has pushed through nearly 100 trillion lire ($60 billion) of deficit-cutting measures since taking office in May 1996 in the name of monetary union.

But he has yet to tackle tough social spending reforms that analysts say will be vital to keeping the books balanced. The government is due to open talks with trades unions and employers on reform of the welfare state on Wednesday.

Corriere cautioned: "The danger which has been avoided in Amsterdam does not minimise the challenges which await us, it increases them. And lowering our guard...would be the most serious, the most fatal of errors".
